rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
$$Z=\frac{PV}{nRT}\ \ (Z=1\ \text{ideal},\ Z<1\ \text{attraction},\ Z>1\ \text{finite volume})$$
$$\left(P+\frac{an^{2}}{V^{2}}\right)(V-nb)=nRT$$
$$V_{c}=3b,\quad P_{c}=\frac{a}{27b^{2}},\quad T_{c}=\frac{8a}{27Rb},\quad Z_{c}=\frac{P_{c}V_{c}}{RT_{c}}=\frac{3}{8}$$

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ A real gas always has Z > 1. ✅ Z < 1 at moderate pressure (attraction dominates) and Z > 1 at high pressure (molecular volume dominates); hydrogen is a special case with Z > 1 throughout.  ·  ❌ Deviation from ideality increases as temperature rises. ✅ It decreases with rising temperature and increases at high pressure and low temperature.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: Zc(observed) for most gases lies between 0.23 and 0.31, below the van der Waals value 0.375.  ·  Hydrogen and helium have the smallest a and b values and stay closest to ideal behaviour; SO₂ and CO₂ deviate most among common gases.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: **Problem:** Compute Z for 1 mol of gas at 300 K occupying 0.5 L at 50 atm. **Solution:** Z = PV/RT = (50 × 0.5)/(0.0821 × 300) ≈ 1.015 → slightly greater than 1, so the finite molecular volume effect dominates.  ·  **Problem:** For a gas with a = 3.6 L² atm mol⁻² and b = 0.043 L mol⁻¹, find Tc and Pc. **Solution:** Tc = 8a/27Rb = (8 × 3.6)/(27 × 0.0821 × 0.043) ≈ 302 K; Pc = a/27b² = 3.6/(27 × 0.043²) ≈ 72 atm.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: deviation of real gas from ideality, solving related numerical problems based on gas laws (within States of Matter).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ### 1. Meaning of deviation  ·  A real gas obeys PV = nRT only approximately; the departure from that equation is called deviation from ideal behaviour. It arises because the two postulates of the kinetic theory are only idealisations — molecules do occupy volume, and intermolecular attractive forces do exist (otherwise no gas could ever be liquefied).…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Critical temperatures: He −268 °C, N₂ −147 °C, CO₂ 31 °C, water 374 °C — the reason He is the hardest gas to liquefy.  ·  Ideal gas equation PV = nRT; from kinetic theory P = ⅓ (Nm/m)⟨c²⟩, so PV = ⅓N m⟨c²⟩.

rows.text: ### 2. Compressibility factor Z  ·  $Z=\frac{PV}{nRT}$ (or Z = PV/RT for one mole) measures deviation: Z = 1 for an ideal gas, **Z < 1** when attraction dominates (moderate pressure, gas easier to compress than ideal), **Z > 1** when the finite molecular volume dominates (high pressure, gas harder to compress than ideal).…  ·  ### 3. rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: $$P_{r}=\frac{P}{P_{c}},\quad V_{r}=\frac{V}{V_{c}},\quad T_{r}=\frac{T}{T_{c}}$$  ·  PV = nRT  ·  c_rms = √(3RT/M)

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: KE_mole = 3RT/2  ·  ❌ The constant b is the molecular volume. ✅ b is the excluded volume per mole, about four times the actual molecular volume.  ·  ❌ Gases can always be liquefied by increasing pressure. ✅ Above the critical temperature no amount of pressure can liquefy a gas.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ Zc = 0.375 is exact for all gases. ✅ It is the van der Waals *prediction*; experiment gives 0.23–0.31, which is a limitation of the equation.  ·  ❌ skip the key fact → ✅ ideal gas equation pv = nrt; from kinetic theory p = ⅓ (nm/m)⟨c²⟩, so pv = ⅓n m⟨c²⟩..  ·  State that the van der Waals equation explains the critical point only approximately — Zc = 0.375 versus experimental 0.23–0.31.
